    def test_data_stats(metrics, submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats):
        """Check the converted dataset matches the reference in size, variables and ranges.
    
        Records every statistic into `metrics` first, so a failing run still reports what
        it produced, then compares against the reference solution within STATLIMITS:
    
          * subject count must match exactly; session, trial, neuron counts and median
            trial length within 10%
          * decoder inputs and outputs are matched to the reference by name similarity
            and value range, so producing the right NUMBER of variables but the wrong
            ones fails rather than passes
          * per-output class counts and class fractions must match, since a different
            discretisation makes decoder accuracies incomparable
    
        Skips rather than fails when reference stats are unavailable, so the test is
        still useful for recording metrics on a task with no reference yet.
        """
    
        fields_check = [
            'nsessions',
            'ntrials_total',
            'T_median',
            'nsubjects',
            'nneurons_total',
        ]
    
        # Always record the raw submitted counts, even when there's no reference to
        # compare against — the numbers themselves are useful for downstream
        # reporting / grids.
        for field in fields_check:
            metrics[field] = submitted_data_stats[field]
    
        # Record per-variable n_classes for the agent's outputs. We do this BEFORE
        # the reference-availability check because the value doesn't depend on a
        # reference, and downstream (e.g. chance-baselined / informedness plots)
        # need it for unsupervised tasks too.
        sub_output_range = submitted_data_stats.get('output_range', {})
        for var, (lo, hi) in sub_output_range.items():
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_{var}'] = int(round(hi))+1
    
        # Per-variable input range — also recorded BEFORE the skip so unsupervised
        # tasks have it. Inputs aren't necessarily integer-coded, so we record the
        # endpoints as [lo, hi] rather than an n_classes count.
        sub_input_range = submitted_data_stats.get('input_range', {})
        for var, (lo, hi) in sub_input_range.items():
            metrics[f'input_range_{var}'] = [float(lo), float(hi)]
    
        # Also record the raw counts (dinput / doutput) — same rationale.
        metrics['dinput']  = int(submitted_data_stats.get('dinput', 0))
        metrics['doutput'] = int(submitted_data_stats.get('doutput', 0))
    
        if reference_data_stats is None:
            pytest.skip("Reference data stats not available for comparison")
            return
    
        for field in fields_check:
            metrics[field+'_ratio'] = submitted_data_stats[field] / reference_data_stats['data_summary'][field]
            # Verdict recorded where the threshold is applied; the assert below reads it back.
            # The assert loop bails on its first failure, so computing these here is what makes
            # a later field's result knowable after an earlier one has failed.
            metrics[field+'_ok'] = bool(
                ratio_within_limits(metrics[field+'_ratio'], STATLIMITS[field+'_ratio']))
    
        # Seed a per-variable verdict for every REFERENCE output, so a variable the agent never
        # produced -- and which therefore never appears in output_matches below -- counts as a
        # miss rather than shrinking the denominator of the fraction categories.
        reference_output_names = list(reference_data_stats['data_summary'].get('output_range') or [])
        for ref_name in reference_output_names:
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_ok_{ref_name}'] = False
            metrics[f'output_fraction_ok_{ref_name}'] = False
    
        # check that input ranges match via 1-1 matching
        input_matches, input_match_costs = match_variables_by_hungarian(
            submitted_data_stats['input_range'],
            reference_data_stats['data_summary']['input_range'],
            weight_semantic=.95,
            weight_range=.05,
            weight_fraction=0,
            exact_range=False,
        )
    
        # A task with no decoder inputs (dinput == 0) is valid: there is nothing to
        # match, so there is no mismatch cost. np.mean([]) would be NaN, and every
        # comparison against NaN is False, so the cost assertion below could never pass.
        # Named for what it is: the mean Hungarian MATCHING cost, which is dominated
        # by name similarity and is forced to 0 for exactly-matching names before any
        # range term is computed. It is not a mean of the input_range_error_<var>
        # fields -- that is mean_input_range_error, recorded below.
        mean_input_cost = float(np.mean(input_match_costs)) if len(input_match_costs) else 0.0
        metrics['input_match_mean_cost'] = mean_input_cost
        metrics['input_matches'] = [
            {'reference': ref, 'submitted': sub, 'cost': cost}
            for ref, sub, cost in input_matches
        ]
        sub_input_range = submitted_data_stats['input_range']
        ref_input_range = reference_data_stats['data_summary']['input_range']
        for ref_name, sub_name, _ in input_matches:
            ref_lo, ref_hi = ref_input_range[ref_name]
            sub_lo, sub_hi = sub_input_range[sub_name]
            scale = abs(ref_hi - ref_lo)
            if scale < 1e-6 and abs(sub_hi - sub_lo) < 1e-6:
                metrics[f'input_range_error_{ref_name}'] = 0.0
            else:
                scale = max(scale, 1e-6)
                metrics[f'input_range_error_{ref_name}'] = float(max(abs(ref_lo - sub_lo)/scale, abs(ref_hi - sub_hi)/scale))
        mean_input_range_error = np.mean([metrics[f'input_range_error_{ref_name}'] for ref_name, _, _ in input_matches]) if len(input_matches) else 0.0
        metrics['mean_input_range_error'] = mean_input_range_error
        # Recorded ONLY when there is something to match. A task with no decoder inputs
        # (allen2p: dinput == 0, input_range == {}) has no input ranges to compare, so leaving
        # the key unset scores the category undefined and drops it from the mean -- rather than
        # awarding a free 1.0 for a check that never happened. Matches undefined_categories()
        # in lesion_analysis.py, which singles out this same case. The assert below is guarded
        # by the same condition, so it never reads a key that was not written.
        if len(input_matches):
            metrics['input_range_ok'] = bool(
                mean_input_range_error <= STATLIMITS['input_range_error'])
    
        # match outputs based on range, fraction, and semantic similarity of names
        output_matches, output_match_costs = match_outputs(
            submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats
        )
        metrics['output_matches'] = [
            {'reference': ref, 'submitted': sub, 'cost': cost}
            for ref, sub, cost in output_matches
        ]
    
        # As above: the mean matching cost, not a mean of output_fraction_error_<var>.
        mean_output_match_cost = float(np.mean(output_match_costs))
        metrics['output_match_mean_cost'] = mean_output_match_cost
        sub_output_range = submitted_data_stats['output_range']
        ref_output_range = reference_data_stats['data_summary']['output_range']
        for ref_name, sub_name, _ in output_matches:
            ref_lo, ref_hi = ref_output_range[ref_name]
            sub_lo, sub_hi = sub_output_range[sub_name]
            metrics[f'output_range_error_{ref_name}'] = float(abs(sub_hi - ref_hi))
            # Record the number of output classes per variable, so consumers can
            # derive chance level (= 1 / n_classes) for chance-baselined metrics.
            # For integer-coded categorical outputs, n_classes = hi + 1.
            # `output_nclasses_<var>` is the submitted (agent) value; the
            # `_reference_<var>` variant is the reference's n_classes.
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_{ref_name}'] = int(round(sub_hi) + 1)
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_reference_{ref_name}'] = int(round(ref_hi) + 1)
            # fraction error per output
            ref_fracs = sorted(reference_data_stats['data_summary']['output_fractions'][ref_name].values())
            sub_fracs = sorted(submitted_data_stats['output_fractions'][sub_name].values())
            if len(ref_fracs) == len(sub_fracs):
                metrics[f'output_fraction_error_{ref_name}'] = float(np.sum(np.abs(np.array(ref_fracs) - np.array(sub_fracs))))
            else:
                metrics[f'output_fraction_error_{ref_name}'] = None
    
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_ok_{ref_name}'] = bool(
                metrics[f'output_range_error_{ref_name}'] <= STATLIMITS['output_range_error'])
            # A None error means the class counts differ, so there is no comparable fraction
            # vector. That scores as a miss, but is NOT asserted on below -- the nclasses check
            # already fails that case, and asserting here too would change what the suite
            # rejects. Verdict and assert diverge only here, deliberately.
            frac_error = metrics[f'output_fraction_error_{ref_name}']
            metrics[f'output_fraction_ok_{ref_name}'] = bool(
                frac_error is not None and frac_error <= STATLIMITS['output_fraction_error'])

    def test_decoder_accuracy(metrics, submitted_data_full, submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats):
        """Run the provided train_decoder.py script on the data and check that it runs without error."""
    
        from decoder import (
            get_trial_indices,
            train_validate_decoder,
            accuracy_all_sessions
        )
        import torch
    
        train_params = {
            'npcs': 100,
            'lr': 1e-3,
            'l1_weight': 1e-4,
            'balanced_loss': True,
        }
    
        metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy'] = None
    
        if reference_data_stats is not None:
            ref_accuracy = reference_data_stats['validation_balanced_accuracy']
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_reference'] = ref_accuracy
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_ratio'] = None
            # Seeded False for every reference output, as in test_data_stats: an output the
            # agent never produced is a miss, not an absent denominator. Seeded here rather
            # than after training so the verdicts exist even if training itself raises.
            for ref_name in (reference_data_stats['data_summary'].get('output_range') or []):
                metrics[f'decoder_accuracy_ok_{ref_name}'] = False
    
        # train the decoder on the submitted data
        rng_state = reference_data_stats.get("rng_state") if reference_data_stats else None
        try:
            scores, predictions, pcs, confidences, train_idx, test_idx, model, output, _ = \
                train_validate_decoder(submitted_data_full['neural'], submitted_data_full['input'],
                                    submitted_data_full['output'], state=rng_state, **train_params)
        except torch.cuda.OutOfMemoryError:
            print("CUDA out of memory error during decoder training. Retrying on CPU...")
            train_params['device'] = torch.device('cpu')
            scores, predictions, pcs, confidences, train_idx, test_idx, model, output, _ = \
                train_validate_decoder(submitted_data_full['neural'], submitted_data_full['input'],
                                    submitted_data_full['output'], state=rng_state, **train_params)
    
        # evaluate accuracy on test set
        test_predictions_only = get_trial_indices(predictions, test_idx)
        test_output_only = get_trial_indices(output, test_idx)
        balanced_accuracy = accuracy_all_sessions(test_predictions_only, test_output_only, balanced=True)
    
        sub_accuracy = {
            submitted_data_full['output_names'][i]: float(balanced_accuracy[i])
            for i in range(len(balanced_accuracy))
        }
        # Persist the raw per-output accuracy as soon as it's computed. Everything
        # below can raise or assert, so anything done afterwards must not be
        # required to preserve this field.
        metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy'] = sub_accuracy
    
        if reference_data_stats is None:
            pytest.skip("Reference data stats not available for comparison, skipping accuracy ratio and threshold checks")
            return
    
        # The matching + ratio + threshold checks below are wrapped so that a
        # failure there doesn't prevent the raw accuracy above from being reported.
        # Any error is re-raised at the end so the test still fails visibly, but
        # not before the metric has been recorded.
        deferred_error = None
        try:
            # find a match between output dimensions (same as test_data_stats)
            output_matches, _ = match_outputs(
                submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats
            )
            # The mean of those costs is deliberately NOT recorded here. test_data_stats
            # already writes it as output_match_mean_cost from the same match_outputs
            # call, and a second copy only drifts: this one is written solely by a
            # decoder retrain, so after any reference change it lags the first. That is
            # exactly what happened to sosa2024, where the old copy was averaged over
            # the 3 outputs the reference had at the time rather than today's 6.
    
            # Best-effort ratio: skip any match whose reference or submitted name
            # isn't resolvable (e.g. matcher returned inf cost / None).
            ratio = {}
            for ref_name, sub_name, cost in output_matches:
                if sub_name is None or sub_name not in sub_accuracy:
                    continue
                if ref_name is None or ref_name not in ref_accuracy or not ref_accuracy[ref_name]:
                    continue
                ratio[ref_name] = sub_accuracy[sub_name] / ref_accuracy[ref_name]
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_ratio'] = ratio
    
            # Recorded so a failure can be read without recomputing anything: the bar each
            # output had to clear.
            thresholds = {}
    
            # Two passes, deliberately. The assert loop stops at the first output below
            # threshold, so recording every verdict first is what makes the remaining outputs'
            # results knowable -- otherwise one bad output would hide the other five.
            for ref_name, sub_name, _ in output_matches:
                if sub_name is None or sub_name not in sub_accuracy:
                    continue
                if ref_name is None or ref_name not in ref_accuracy:
                    continue
                threshold = accuracy_threshold(ref_name, reference_data_stats)
                thresholds[ref_name] = threshold
                metrics[f'decoder_accuracy_ok_{ref_name}'] = bool(
                    sub_accuracy[sub_name] >= threshold)
            # Written before the asserts, so a failing output's bar is on record too.
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_threshold'] = thresholds
    
            for ref_name, sub_name, _ in output_matches:
                if sub_name is None or sub_name not in sub_accuracy:
                    continue
                if ref_name is None or ref_name not in ref_accuracy:
                    continue
                sub_acc = sub_accuracy[sub_name]
                threshold = thresholds[ref_name]
                mean = reference_data_stats['validation_balanced_accuracy_mean'][ref_name]
                std = reference_data_stats['validation_balanced_accuracy_std'][ref_name]
                assert metrics[f'decoder_accuracy_ok_{ref_name}'], (
                    f'Accuracy for output {sub_name} ({sub_acc:.3f}) is below reference mean '
                    f'{mean:.3f} - {ACCURACY_NSTD:g}*std {std:.3f} = {threshold:.3f}')
        except BaseException as e:  # AssertionError or anything raised by the matcher
            deferred_error = e
    
        if deferred_error is not None:
>           raise deferred_error

Your goal is to load and reformat data from a neuroscience paper into a specified structure suitable for downstream analysis.\n- You need to use the **SAME** processing of the data described in the provided reference papers and code repository when applicable. This requires examining the provided papers, code, and data to understand how the data is formatted and processed, and determine how to balance this with the requirements of the new downstream analysis.\n- To test that you have done this successfully, you will use provided code to train a neural decoder that **inputs neural activity** and **predicts experimental and behavioral variables**. \n- We will assess your work in two ways. First, statistics of the converted data and decoder accuracy will be compared to those of an expert-written solution. Second, each decision you make about how to load, filter, process, align, and save the data will be compared with the decision made by an expert. A decision that differs from the expert's is acceptable if it is equally well justified; decisions that are poorly justified will be flagged as concerning or incorrect.\n\n## Reference Information\n\n- Reference **papers**:\n  - The whitepaper about the dataset, \"Allen Brain Observatory: Visual Behavior 2P Technical Whitepaper\", is in the file `/app/whitepaper.pdf`.\n  - A paper using this dataset, \"Behavioral strategy shapes activation of the Vip-Sst disinhibitory circuit in visual cortex\", is in the file `/app/paper.pdf`.\n- Some parts of the paper that describe the experiment and processing have been copied to the file `/app/methods.txt`. \n- **Code**:\n  - The Allen data **SDK** is in the directory `/app/code`.\n  - Tutorials about using the data are in the directory `/app/tutorials`.\n- **Data** from the paper are in the directory `/app/data`.\n- **Documentation** on using this dataset is at https://allensdk.readthedocs.io/en/latest/visual_behavior_optical_physiology.html\n\n## Decoder Task\n\n- Collect and convert data under the \"Visual Behavior\" task.\n- Temporally align based on ophys timestamp.\n- Segment each recording session into individual trials based on how they are defined in the experiment. Include both the \"Go\" and \"Catch\" trials, but exclude the \"Aborted\" and \"Auto-rewarded\" trials.\n\n### Decoder Inputs:\n\nNo inputs for this task.\n\n### Decoder Outputs\n\n- Image identity (of the image presented during the non-grey screen), categorical variable. Time-varying.\n- Image change, binary variable. Have value of 1 right after a change in image identity, otherwise 0. Time-varying.\n- Running speed, discretized into five equal percentile bins. Time-varying.\n- Pupil diameter, discretized into five equal percentile bins.  Time-varying.\n- Trial outcome. Static per-trial.\n\n## Target Data Format\n\n- Save the full converted dataset to the pickle file `/app/converted_data.pkl`.\n- All datasets must be converted into the following Python dictionary structure:\n\n```python\ndata = {\n    'neural': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # shape: (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # trial 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        [  # list of trials for session 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'input': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'output': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'subjects': list of str, # ids of all subjects, length n_subjects\n    'subject_idx': shape (n_sessions,), # index into subjects for each session\n\n    'brain_regions': list of str, # names of the brain regions recorded from, e.g. ALM, V1\n    'brain_region_idx': [ # list of sessions\n        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\n    ], # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\n\n    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\n    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\n    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\n        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'metadata': {\n        'task_description': str, # description of output tasks\n        'time_bin_size': float, # length of time bin in ms\n        'temporal_alignment_event': str, # description of alignment event\n        'off_start': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        ...\n    }\n}\n```\n\n### Key Format Requirements\n\n- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\n  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\n  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \n  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\n\n- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\n  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \n  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\n  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\n\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\n\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \n\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\n\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \n  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\n  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\n\n## Python environment\n\n- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\n- Use `python3` to run any python code.\n- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\n\n## Decoder Reference\n\n- Run this script with `python /app/train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\n- Optional arguments:\n  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\n  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\n  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\n- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\n\n### Purpose\n\nThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\n1. Data structure is correct - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n2. Dimensions are consistent - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n3. Values are sensible - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n4. Decoder can successfully train and predict\n5. Poor performance indicates data formatting issues that need investigation\n\n### Consistency requirements\n\nYour processing and formatting must **match the reference papers and code** with respect to:\n- Loading of data\n- Temporal alignment of different time series streams (neural, inputs, outputs)\n- Processing of neural, input, and output data streams\n- Curation of data: filtering of low-quality neurons, trials, sessions, and mice.\n\nTo check consistency, you must compare statistics available in the reference papers and your converted dataset. \n\nWhenever possible, invent **SANITY CHECKS** that your loading and processing matches the reference papers and code. \n\nDiscrepancies are only allowed if required by the Decoder Input and Decoder Output specifications above, or the task of training a neural decoder.\n\nCarefully verify your work after every step. When you find mistakes, document and fix them immediately. Be critical of results **after every step of processing**. \n\nYou will be assessed on whether the decisions you make on how to load, filter, process, align, reformat, and save the data are reasonable and match the reference papers and code and these instructions. During testing, the reference version of `/app/train_decoder.py` will be run on your converted data. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \n  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\n  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\n\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\n\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \n\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\n\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \n  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\n  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\n\n## Python environment\n\n- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\n- Use `python3` to run any python code.\n- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\n\n## Decoder Reference\n\n- Run this script with `python /app/train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\n- Optional arguments:\n  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\n  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\n  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\n- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\n\n### Purpose\n\nThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\n1. Data structure is correct - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n2. Dimensions are consistent - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n3. Values are sensible - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n4. Decoder can successfully train and predict\n5. Poor performance indicates data formatting issues that need investigation\n\n### Consistency requirements\n\nYour processing and formatting must **match the reference papers and code** with respect to:\n- Loading of data\n- Temporal alignment of different time series streams (neural, inputs, outputs)\n- Processing of neural, input, and output data streams\n- Curation of data: filtering of low-quality neurons, trials, sessions, and mice.\n\nTo check consistency, you must compare statistics available in the reference papers and your converted dataset. \n\nWhenever possible, invent **SANITY CHECKS** that your loading and processing matches the reference papers and code. \n\nDiscrepancies are only allowed if required by the Decoder Input and Decoder Output specifications above, or the task of training a neural decoder.\n\nCarefully verify your work after every step. When you find mistakes, document and fix them immediately. Time-varying.\n49\t- Image change, binary variable. Have value of 1 right after a change in image identity, otherwise 0. Time-varying.\n50\t- Running speed, discretized into five equal percentile bins. Time-varying.\n51\t- Pupil diameter, discretized into five equal percentile bins.  Time-varying.\n52\t- Trial outcome. Static per-trial.\n53\t\n54\t## Target Data Format\n55\t\n56\t- Save the full converted dataset to the pickle file `/app/converted_data.pkl`.\n57\t- All datasets must be converted into the following Python dictionary structure:\n58\t\n59\t```python\n60\tdata = {\n61\t    'neural': [  # list of sessions\n62\t        [  # list of trials for session 1\n63\t            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # shape: (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\n64\t            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # trial 2\n65\t            ...\n66\t        ],\n67\t        [  # list of trials for session 2\n68\t            ...\n69\t        ],\n70\t        ...\n71\t    ],\n72\t\n73\t    'input': [  # list of sessions\n74\t        [  # list of trials for session 1\n75\t            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\n76\t            ...\n77\t        ],\n78\t        ...\n79\t    ],\n80\t\n81\t    'output': [  # list of sessions\n82\t        [  # list of trials for session 1\n83\t            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\n84\t            ...\n85\t        ],\n86\t        ...\n87\t    ],\n88\t\n89\t    'subjects': list of str, # ids of all subjects, length n_subjects\n90\t    'subject_idx': shape (n_sessions,), # index into subjects for each session\n91\t\n92\t    'brain_regions': list of str, # names of the brain regions recorded from, e.g. ALM, V1\n93\t    'brain_region_idx': [ # list of sessions\n94\t        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\n95\t    ], # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\n96\t\n97\t    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\n98\t    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\n99\t    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\n100\t        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\n101\t        ...\n102\t    ],\n103\t\n104\t    'metadata': {\n105\t        'task_description': str, # description of output tasks\n106\t        'time_bin_size': float, # length of time bin in ms\n107\t        'temporal_alignment_event': str, # description of alignment event\n108\t        'off_start': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n109\t        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n110\t        ...\n111\t    }\n112\t}\n113\t```\n114\t\n115\t### Key Format Requirements\n116\t\n117\t- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\n118\t  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\n119\t  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \n120\t  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\n121\t\n122\t- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\n123\t  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n124\t  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n125\t    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n126\t    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n127\t    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n128\t  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n129\t  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n130\t  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n131\t\n132\t- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n133\t  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\n134\t  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \n135\t  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\n136\t  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\n137\t  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \n138\t\n139\t- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\n140\t- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\n141\t  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\n142\t\n143\t- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\n144\t- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\n145\t\n146\t- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\n147\t  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \n148\t\n149\t- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\n150\t  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\n151\t- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\n152\t  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\n153\t\n154\t- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \n155\t  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\n156\t  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\n157\t  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \n158\t  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\n159\t  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\n160\t\n161\t## Python environment\n162\t\n163\t- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\n164\t- Use `python3` to run any python code.\n165\t- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\n166\t\n167\t## Decoder Reference\n168\t\n169\t- Run this script with `python /app/train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\n170\t- Optional arguments:\n171\t  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\n172\t  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\n173\t  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\n174\t- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\n175\t\n176\t### Purpose\n177\t\n178\tThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\n179\t1. Data structure is correct - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n180\t2. Dimensions are consistent - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n181\t3. Values are sensible - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n182\t4. Decoder can successfully train and predict\n183\t5. Poor performance indicates data formatting issues that need investigation\n184\t\n185\t### Consistency requirements\n186\t\n187\tYour processing and formatting must **match the reference papers and code** with respect to:\n188\t- Loading of data\n189\t- Temporal alignment of different time series streams (neural, inputs, outputs)\n190\t- Processing of neural, input, and output data streams\n191\t- Curation of data: filtering of low-quality neurons, trials, sessions, and mice.\n192\t\n193\tTo check consistency, you must compare statistics available in the reference papers and your converted dataset. \n194\t\n195\tWhenever possible, invent **SANITY CHECKS** that your loading and processing matches the reference papers and code. \n196\t\n197\tDiscrepancies are only allowed if required by the Decoder Input and Decoder Output specifications above, or the task of training a neural decoder.\n198\t\n199\tCarefully verify your work after every step. When you find mistakes, document and fix them immediately. Be critical of results **after every step of processing**. \n200\t\n201\tYou will be assessed on whether the decisions you make on how to load, filter, process, align, reformat, and save the data are reasonable and match the reference papers and code and these instructions. During testing, the reference version of `/app/train_decoder.py` will be run on your converted data. Data statistics and decoder accuracy will be compared to those achieved by human-written conversion code. \n202\t\n203\t---\n204\t\n205\t## Conversion Workflow\n206\t\n207\t**IMPORTANT**: Follow these steps in order. list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'subjects': list of str, # They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. Trials are defined using the built-in `dataset.trials` table from the Allen SDK. Each trial corresponds to one stimulus change event (go or catch). The full trial window from `start_time` to `stop_time` is used, giving variable-length trials (typically ~80-90 frames / ~8s). Aborted trials, auto-rewarded trials, and trials without a valid `change_time` are excluded.\n54\t\n55\tii.\n56\t```python\n57\ttrials_table = ref_ds.trials\n58\t...\n59\tvalid_trials = trials_table[\n60\t    (~trials_table['aborted']) &\n61\t    (~trials_table['auto_rewarded']) &\n62\t    (trials_table['change_time'].notna())\n63\t]\n64\t\n65\tfor _, row in valid_trials.iterrows():\n66\t    start_idx = np.searchsorted(ophys_ts, row['start_time'])\n67\t    end_idx = np.searchsorted(ophys_ts, row['stop_time'])\n68\t    if end_idx > T:\n69\t        end_idx = T\n70\t    if end_idx <= start_idx:\n71\t        continue\n72\t    idx = np.arange(start_idx, end_idx)\n73\t```\n74\t\n75\tiii. The SDK's built-in trials table was used, since it provides pre-computed trial metadata (outcome, image identity, timing). The full trial window (`start_time` to `stop_time`) is used rather than a fixed window around `change_time`, so that the trial includes both pre-change stimulus flashes and the post-change response window. This enables time-varying output variables (image identity changes mid-trial). Trials are typically ~8s: ~4s pre-change (variable number of stimulus flashes) and ~4.2s post-change (fixed response window).\n76\t\n77\t## 1-e. Sessions with fewer than 2 valid trials are excluded from the final output.\n80\t\n81\tii.\n82\t```python\n83\tvalid_trials = trials_table[\n84\t    (~trials_table['aborted']) &\n85\t    (~trials_table['auto_rewarded']) &\n86\t    (trials_table['change_time'].notna())\n87\t]\n88\t...\n89\tif end_idx > T:\n90\t    end_idx = T\n91\tif end_idx <= start_idx:\n92\t    continue\n93\t...\n94\tif len(trials) < 2:\n95\t    continue\n96\t```\n97\t\n98\tiii. Per instruction, we are ignoring aborted and auto-rewarded trials. Aborted trials were excluded because the mouse licked before the change occurred, so no change stimulus was presented. Auto-rewarded trials were excluded because the free reward biases the behavioral response. Requiring a valid `change_time` ensures there is a well-defined change point within the trial. The minimum 2-trial threshold prevents degenerate sessions from entering the dataset.\n99\t\n100\t## 2-a. What variables in the raw data is the final `neural` data derived from?\n101\t\n102\ti. Trials are defined using the built-in `dataset.trials` table from the Allen SDK. Each trial corresponds to one stimulus change event (go or catch). The SDK's built-in trials table was used, since it provides pre-computed trial metadata (outcome, image identity, timing). The full trial window (`start_time` to `stop_time`) is used rather than a fixed window around `change_time`, so that the trial includes both pre-change stimulus flashes and the post-change response window. This enables time-varying output variables (image identity changes mid-trial). Trials are typically ~8s: ~4s pre-change (variable number of stimulus flashes) and ~4.2s post-change (fixed response window).\n\n## 1-e. How are trials filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. Aborted trials (early lick before change), auto-rewarded trials (free reward), and trials without a valid `change_time` are excluded. Trials where `end_idx <= start_idx` (empty window) are skipped. Verified over all 51,992 go+catch trials that this window lies inside [start_time, stop_time] and never runs off the stimulus block.\n181\t- off_start = -2.25 s, off_end = +3.0 s relative to the change (nominal 750 ms spacing).\n182\t- Fixed T = 8 for every trial in every session satisfies the requirement that time bins be the same size for all trials and sessions.\n183\t\n184\t### Variable Mapping\n185\t| Source Variable | Target Field | Transform | Reference Code Function(s) | Notes |\n186\t|-----------------|--------------|-----------|----------------------------|-------|\n187\t| events.events per cell + ophys_timestamps | neural | sum of detected event magnitudes in each 750 ms bin per neuron; Multiscope planes concatenated along neuron axis | .events, .ophys_timestamps | paper uses detected calcium events; each plane binned on its own timestamps |\n188\t| - | input | empty array shape (0, 8) | - | Decoder Task: No inputs for this task. summing is the natural per-bin aggregate and keeps rigs with different frame rates comparable.\n200\t3. **Merge Multiscope planes into one session**: simultaneously recorded from one animal on one clock, so they form one population.\n201\t4. **Exclude passive sessions**: 0 licks / 0 rewards makes trial outcome degenerate.\n202\t5. **Exclude aborted and auto-rewarded trials**: required by the Decoder Task and consistent with the whitepaper analysis.\n203\t6. **All outputs time-varying**: image identity, change, running and pupil vary within a trial; trial outcome is constant per trial but broadcast across bins, per the instruction to make outputs time-varying if at all possible.\n204\t7. **Within-session quintile edges for running and pupil**: pupil width is measured in camera pixels whose scale depends on the per-session camera alignment, and running propensity differs enormously between animals, so a single global edge set would mostly encode which session/mouse a trial came from rather than the animal state. Computing the five equal-percentile edges within each session makes each class mean the same thing (relative level for this animal on this day) everywhere, and yields exactly ~20% per class both per session and overall (verified: 0.199-0.202).\n205\t8. **Drop the 3 sessions lacking eye tracking** rather than emit NaN, which verify_data_format rejects.\n206\t\n207\t### Planned Sanity Checks\n208\t- [ ] change_time coincides exactly with a flash onset for every kept trial (verified globally already).\n209\t- [ ] The 8-bin window lies inside [start_time, stop_time] for every kept trial (verified globally already).\n210\t- [ ] Trial counts: kept go+catch == 51,992 minus trials of dropped no-eye-tracking sessions.\n211\t- [ ] image_change has exactly one 1 per trial, always at bin index 3.\n212\t- [ ] Image identity at bin 3 equals trials.change_image_name; at bin 2 equals trials.initial_image_name.\n213\t- [ ] Outcome distribution reproduces hit 15,936 / miss 29,541 / FA 931 / CR 5,584 before session drops.\n214\t- [ ] Running and pupil classes each hold about 20% of timepoints.\n215\t- [ ] Neural spot check: recompute binned events for a specific (session, trial, neuron) straight from the raw NWB and compare with np.allclose.\n216\t- [ ] Total neurons over kept sessions equals the sum of valid ROIs of kept experiments.\n217\t\n218\t\n219\t---\n220\t\n221\t---\n222\t\n223\t## Step 6: Script Development\n224\t**Status**: COMPLETE\n225\t\n226\t`/app/convert_data.py` implements the Step 5 mapping. Structure:\n227\t- `get_session_table()` - intersects `ophys_experiment_table.csv` with the NWB files actually on disk, drops passive experiments, and groups experiments by `ophys_session_id` so that Multiscope planes become one session.\n228\t- `process_session()` - loads each plane with `BehaviorOphysExperiment.from_nwb_path`, takes the behaviour streams from the first plane (verified identical across planes), selects go+catch trials, finds each trial's change flash, bins every stream, and returns arrays.\n229\t- `binned_sum()` / `binned_mean_1d()` - cumulative-sum + `searchsorted` binning, so each stream is traversed once regardless of the number of bins.\n230\t- `quantile_bin()` - 5 equal-percentile classes.\n231\t- `plot_processing()` - the `--show-processing` figures.\n232\t- `main()` - pools sessions over workers, builds shared vocabularies, assembles the dict, pickles it.\n233\t\n234\tOptions: `--full` (default), `--sample` (1 single-plane + 1 Multiscope session, so both rig types are exercised), `--show-processing`, `--workers`.\n235\t\n236\tCode inefficiencies identified:\n237\t- Naively looping over bins and re-scanning the event array per bin would be O(n_bins x n_frames). Replaced with one cumulative sum per plane plus `searchsorted` lookups.\n238\t- Loading each NWB more than once (e.g. once for behaviour and once for neural) would double the IO. Each plane is loaded exactly once and the behaviour streams are read only from the first plane.\n239\t\n240\tCode speedups added:\n241\t- `multiprocessing.Pool` over sessions (sessions are independent).\n242\t- cumsum/searchsorted binning as above.\n243\t- float32 neural output to halve memory.\n244\t\n245\t### Bug found and fixed during development\n246\tThe first run asserted `chg[:, N_PRE] == 1` for every trial and failed. Investigation showed this was my error, not a data problem: `stimulus_presentations.is_change` marks only **real** image changes, and on **catch** trials the change_time marks a *sham* change where the image does not actually change. This is exactly the semantics the Decoder Task wants for `image_change` (1 only after a genuine change in image identity), so catch trials are legitimately all-zero. The assertion was rewritten to require `is_change == 1` at the change bin on go trials and `== 0` on catch trials, which now passes for every trial in every session.\n247\t\n248\t---\n249\t\n250\t## Step 7: Sample Conversion and Validation\n251\t**Status**: COMPLETE\n252\t\n253\tCommand: `python -u /app/convert_data.py /app/sample_data.pkl --sample --show-processing`\n254\t\n255\t### Sample Statistics\n256\t| Statistic | Value |\n257\t|-----------|-------|\n258\t| Sessions | 2 (775289198 single-plane; 951410079 Multiscope, 7 planes merged) |\n259\t| Neurons (total) | 177 (89 + 88) |\n260\t| Neurons / session | 89, 88 |\n261\t| Subjects | 2 |\n262\t| Trials (total) | 248 (39 + 209), 0 dropped |\n263\t| Trials / session | 39, 209 |\n264\t| T per trial | 8 bins, all trials |\n265\t| input | shape (0, 8) - no inputs, as specified |\n266\t| image_identity distribution | 8 images each 0.10-0.14, omitted 0.031 |\n267\t| image_change distribution | [0.892, 0.108] |\n268\t| running_speed distribution | [0.201, 0.200, 0.200, 0.200, 0.201] |\n269\t| pupil_diameter distribution | [0.201, 0.200, 0.200, 0.200, 0.201] |\n270\t| trial_outcome distribution | [hit 0.383, miss 0.484, FA 0.036, CR 0.097] |\n271\t| Brain regions | VISp 125, VISl 52 |\n272\t\n273\tThe low trial count of session 775289198 was checked against the raw trials table rather than assumed to be a bug: that session really has 1,078 aborted trials out of 1,117 (an unusually impulsive mouse) leaving only 39 go+catch, and it is the minimum over the whole dataset. Restricting to N>=20 would keep 98.5% of neurons while dropping ~19% of trials, and would very likely raise every reported accuracy.\n478\t\n479\t**Decision: I did not apply a neuron-count filter.** No reference text specifies a minimum-neuron criterion for this dataset; the documented curation is the ROI-validity filter, which is already applied via `exclude_invalid_rois=True`. These are genuine recordings of valid ROIs, and the low accuracy in small populations is a real scientific property (few cells carry little decodable information), not an artifact. Removing ~20% of real trials *because they decode poorly* would optimise the reported score rather than the fidelity of the conversion, and would misrepresent the dataset. The evidence is documented here so the trade-off is explicit and the filter can be applied downstream if a user wants it.\n480\t\n481\tTwo further structural reasons the weaker outputs are bounded:\n482\t- **trial_outcome** is constant within a trial, so the decoder must infer it from 8 bins that include 3 pre-change bins carrying no outcome information at all; and the classes are very unbalanced (FA is 1.9% of trials). 14 sessions do not even contain all four outcome classes (12 have 3, 2 have 2) -- a real property of behaviour.\n483\t- **pupil_diameter** is an arousal variable only indirectly reflected in V1/LM activity, and is quantised within session, so the classes are by construction equally likely and cannot be won by a prior.\n484\t\n485\t### Check 2: Accuracy comparison to papers\n486\t| Variable | My validation accuracy | Paper's reported value |\n487\t|---|---|---|\n488\t| image change (change vs repeat) | 0.658 balanced | Figure 6A, **graphical only** -- no numeric value printed in the text; text states changes \"could be decoded equally well for all cell classes\" |\n489\t| hit vs miss | not decoded separately; `trial_outcome` (4-class) = 0.318 | Figure 6C, graphical only; higher for visual than timing sessions |\n490\t| false alarm | part of `trial_outcome`; FA is the rarest class | text: \"false alarm decoding performance was very low\" -- **consistent with my result** |\n491\t\n492\tThe papers report no numeric decoding accuracies (all in figures), so no quantitative discrepancy can be established. The qualitative pattern matches: image/change information is robustly decodable, and false-alarm information is weak. Note the paper's decoder is also not comparable in setup -- it used a random forest on the first 400 ms after each presentation, per imaging plane, sampling n neurons, whereas this task uses a shared linear decoder on 100 PCs over 750 ms bins across all sessions.\n493\t\n494\t### Check 3: Train vs validation gap\n495\t| Output | Train | Val | Ratio |\n496\t|---|---|---|---|\n497\t| image_identity | 0.534 | 0.490 | 1.09 |\n498\t| image_change | 0.727 | 0.658 | 1.10 |\n499\t| running_speed | 0.385 | 0.316 | 1.22 |\n500\t| pupil_diameter | 0.368 | 0.283 | 1.30 |\n501\t| trial_outcome | 0.518 | 0.318 | 1.63 |\n502\t\n503\tAll but `trial_outcome` are well under 1.5x. `trial_outcome` at 1.63x reflects mild overfitting, expected for a per-trial label with only ~44k trials, strong class imbalance, and a per-session projection with many parameters for small sessions. It is not data leakage: the label is constant within a trial and the train/validation split is by trial, so no bin of a validation trial is ever seen in training.\n504\t\n505\t### Issues Found and Verified: `valid_roi` is True for 100% of returned cells.\n- No further per-neuron filtering is described for this dataset; unlike ephys there are no spike-sorting quality metrics.\n\n**Trial curation rules**:\n- Keep go and catch trials; exclude aborted and auto_rewarded, per the Decoder Task and consistent with the whitepaper which excludes aborted trials from performance metrics and states auto-rewarded trials should not be categorized as hit/miss.\n- Exclude passive sessions (OPHYS_2 / OPHYS_5): verified they contain 0 licks and 0 rewards, so every outcome is miss/correct-reject by construction and trial outcome carries no behavioral information.\n\n### Decoders Trained\n| Decoded variable | Accuracy |\n|---|---|\n| change vs repeat (random forest, 400 ms window, per imaging plane) | reported only graphically in Figure 6A; text says decoded equally well for all cell classes |\n| hit vs miss (random forest) | Figure 6C, graphical only; higher for visual than timing sessions |\n| false alarm decoding | very low (Figure S22) |\n\nNo numeric decoding accuracies appear in the text, so the paper gives qualitative targets: image-change decoding clearly above chance, hit/miss above chance but weaker.\n\n---\n\n## Step 4: Check for Consistency\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n### Discrepancies Found\n| Topic | Code says | Data shows | Papers say | Resolution |\n|-------|-----------|------------|------------|------------|\n| Neural signal | SDK exposes dff_traces, events (detected events), filtered_events (events convolved with causal half-normal, scale 2/31 s, 20 steps) | events sparse (~0.3-1.4% of frames nonzero) | paper: we used the detected calcium events | Use **events**, summed within each 750 ms bin. For training a decoder we keep all active sessions from both rigs and all experience levels: more data, and the Decoder Task does not ask for the novelty/strategy contrast. Deliberate, documented difference. |\n| Trial alignment | change_time from Trial.add_change_time | change_time coincides exactly (0.000000 s) with a flash onset on every go and catch trial | change / sham change is the event the animal reports | Align trials to change_time. |\n| Pupil measure | SDK gives pupil_area, pupil_width, pupil_height | pupil_area is NaN exactly where likely_blink is True | paper does not decode pupil | Use **pupil_width as diameter** (area is an ellipse area, not a diameter; width correlates 0.986 with area). Interpolate across blinks within session before binning. |\n| Omitted flashes | image_name == omitted | omitted flashes always flanked by the same image, never adjacent to a change | omissions are a continuation of the gray screen | Give omissions their own image-identity category rather than dropping or filling them, so no timepoint is fabricated. |\n\nAll three sources agree once the above are resolved. The measured catch fraction (12.5%) independently reproduces the whitepaper catch probability, and measured change-time statistics reproduce the stated design, validating that the trials table is being read as the pipeline wrote it.\n\n---\n\n## Step 5: Mapping Planning\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n### Time base\n- **Bin = one 750 ms image presentation interval**, exactly the unit the paper uses for behavioral analysis.\n- Bin edges come from the actual start_time of consecutive flashes in the change_detection stimulus block, so bins track the real (slightly jittered, 0.73-0.77 s) cadence rather than an idealized grid.\n- **Trial window**: 3 flashes before the change through 4 flashes after, inclusive = **8 bins**. Verified over all 51,992 go+catch trials that this window lies inside [start_time, stop_time] and never runs off the stimulus block.\n- off_start = -2.25 s, off_end = +3.0 s relative to the change (nominal 750 ms spacing).\n- Fixed T = 8 for every trial in every session satisfies the requirement that time bins be the same size for all trials and sessions.\n\n### Variable Mapping\n| Source Variable | Target Field | Transform | Reference Code Function(s) | Notes |\n|-----------------|--------------|-----------|----------------------------|-------|\n| events.events per cell + ophys_timestamps | neural | sum of detected event magnitudes in each 750 ms bin per neuron; Multiscope planes concatenated along neuron axis | .events, .ophys_timestamps | paper uses detected calcium events; each plane binned on its own timestamps |\n| - | input | empty array shape (0, 8) | - | Decoder Task: No inputs for this task. Verified the decoder trains with dinput=0. |\n| stimulus_presentations.image_name | output[0] image_identity | categorical index over a shared 17-value vocabulary (16 images of sets A and B, plus omitted); time-varying | .stimulus_presentations filtered to change_detection block | shared vocabulary keeps the shared readout consistent across sessions |\n| stimulus_presentations.is_change | output[1] image_change | 1 in the bin whose flash is_change, else 0; time-varying | .stimulus_presentations | value 1 right after a change in image identity = the bin beginning at the change flash |\n| running_speed.speed + timestamps | output[2] running_speed_bin | mean speed within each bin, discretized into 5 equal-percentile bins | .running_speed | quintile edges computed WITHIN each session (see Key Decision 7) |\n| eye_tracking.pupil_width + timestamps, likely_blink | output[3] pupil_diameter_bin | blinks (NaN) linearly interpolated within session, mean within bin, then 5 equal-percentile bins | .eye_tracking | 3 experiments (3 sessions) have an empty eye table; those sessions are dropped since outputs cannot be NaN |\n| trials.hit/miss/false_alarm/correct_reject | output[4] trial_outcome | static per trial, broadcast across the 8 bins | .trials | 4 classes; go -> hit/miss, catch -> false_alarm/correct_reject |\n| metadata mouse_id | subjects, subject_idx | unique sorted mouse ids | .metadata | |\n| metadata targeted_structure | brain_regions, brain_region_idx | VISp/VISl per neuron (per plane for Multiscope) | .metadata | Multiscope sessions legitimately span both areas |\n\n### Key Decisions\n1. **Bin 750 ms, 8 bins/trial aligned to change_time**: matches the paper image-presentation interval and guarantees identical T across trials and across both rigs (31 Hz and 11 Hz), which a fixed grid in seconds could not do cleanly.\n2. **Neural = summed detected events per bin**: the paper explicitly uses detected calcium events; summing is the natural per-bin aggregate and keeps rigs with different frame rates comparable.\n3. **Merge Multiscope planes into one session**: simultaneously recorded from one animal on one clock, so they form one population.\n4. **Exclude passive sessions**: 0 licks / 0 rewards makes trial outcome degenerate.\n5. **Exclude aborted and auto-rewarded trials**: required by the Decoder Task and consistent with the whitepaper analysis.\n6. **All outputs time-varying**: image identity, change, running and pupil vary within a trial; trial outcome is constant per trial but broadcast across bins, per the instruction to make outputs time-varying if at all possible.\n7. **Within-session quintile edges for running and pupil**: pupil width is measured in camera pixels whose scale depends on the per-session camera alignment, and running propensity differs enormously between animals, so a single global edge set would mostly encode which session/mouse a trial came from rather than the animal state. Computing the five equal-percentile edges within each session makes each class mean the same thing (relative level for this animal on this day) everywhere, and yields exactly ~20% per class both per session and overall (verified: 0.199-0.202).\n8. **Drop the 3 sessions lacking eye tracking** rather than emit NaN, which verify_data_format rejects.\n\n### Planned Sanity Checks\n- [ ] change_time coincides exactly with a flash onset for every kept trial (verified globally already).\n- [ ] The 8-bin window lies inside [start_time, stop_time] for every kept trial (verified globally already).\n- [ ] Trial counts: kept go+catch == 51,992 minus trials of dropped no-eye-tracking sessions.\n- [ ] image_change has exactly one 1 per trial, always at bin index 3.\n- [ ] Image identity at bin 3 equals trials.change_image_name; at bin 2 equals trials.initial_image_name.\n- [ ] Outcome distribution reproduces hit 15,936 / miss 29,541 / FA 931 / CR 5,584 before session drops.\n- [ ] Running and pupil classes each hold about 20% of timepoints.\n- [ ] Neural spot check: recompute binned events for a specific (session, trial, neuron) straight from the raw NWB and compare with np.allclose.\n- [ ] Total neurons over kept sessions equals the sum of valid ROIs of kept experiments.\n\n\n---\n\n---\n\n## Step 6: Script Development\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n`/app/convert_data.py` implements the Step 5 mapping. Structure:\n- `get_session_table()` - intersects `ophys_experiment_table.csv` with the NWB files actually on disk, drops passive experiments, and groups experiments by `ophys_session_id` so that Multiscope planes become one session.\n- `process_session()` - loads each plane with `BehaviorOphysExperiment.from_nwb_path`, takes the behaviour streams from the first plane (verified identical across planes), selects go+catch trials, finds each trial's change flash, bins every stream, and returns arrays.\n- `binned_sum()` / `binned_mean_1d()` - cumulative-sum + `searchsorted` binning, so each stream is traversed once regardless of the number of bins.\n- `quantile_bin()` - 5 equal-percentile classes.\n- `plot_processing()` - the `--show-processing` figures.\n- `main()` - pools sessions over workers, builds shared vocabularies, assembles the dict, pickles it.\n\nOptions: `--full` (default), `--sample` (1 single-plane + 1 Multiscope session, so both rig types are exercised), `--show-processing`, `--workers`.\n\nCode inefficiencies identified:\n- Naively looping over bins and re-scanning the event array per bin would be O(n_bins x n_frames). Replaced with one cumulative sum per plane plus `searchsorted` lookups.\n- Loading each NWB more than once (e.g. once for behaviour and once for neural) would double the IO. Each plane is loaded exactly once and the behaviour streams are read only from the first plane.\n\nCode speedups added:\n- `multiprocessing.Pool` over sessions (sessions are independent).\n- cumsum/searchsorted binning as above.\n- float32 neural output to halve memory.\n\n### Bug found and fixed during development\nThe first run asserted `chg[:, N_PRE] == 1` for every trial and failed. Investigation showed this was my error, not a data problem: `stimulus_presentations.is_change` marks only **real** image changes, and on **catch** trials the change_time marks a *sham* change where the image does not actually change. This is exactly the semantics the Decoder Task wants for `image_change` (1 only after a genuine change in image identity), so catch trials are legitimately all-zero. The assertion was rewritten to require `is_change == 1` at the change bin on go trials and `== 0` on catch trials, which now passes for every trial in every session.\n\n---\n\n## Step 7: Sample Conversion and Validation\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\nCommand: `python -u /app/convert_data.py /app/sample_data.pkl --sample --show-processing`\n\n### Sample Statistics\n| Statistic | Value |\n|-----------|-------|\n| Sessions | 2 (775289198 single-plane; 951410079 Multiscope, 7 planes merged) |\n| Neurons (total) | 177 (89 + 88) |\n| Neurons / session | 89, 88 |\n| Subjects | 2 |\n| Trials (total) | 248 (39 + 209), 0 dropped |\n| Trials / session | 39, 209 |\n| T per trial | 8 bins, all trials |\n| input | shape (0, 8) - no inputs, as specified |\n| image_identity distribution | 8 images each 0.10-0.14, omitted 0.031 |\n| image_change distribution | [0.892, 0.108] |\n| running_speed distribution | [0.201, 0.200, 0.200, 0.200, 0.201] |\n| pupil_diameter distribution | [0.201, 0.200, 0.200, 0.200, 0.201] |\n| trial_outcome distribution | [hit 0.383, miss 0.484, FA 0.036, CR 0.097] |\n| Brain regions | VISp 125, VISl 52 |\n\nThe low trial count of session 775289198 was checked against the raw trials table rather than assumed to be a bug: that session really has 1,078 aborted trials out of 1,117 (an unusually impulsive mouse) leaving only 39 go+catch, and it is the minimum over the whole dataset. Restricting to N>=20 would keep 98.5% of neurons while dropping ~19% of trials, and would very likely raise every reported accuracy.\n\n**Decision: I did not apply a neuron-count filter.** No reference text specifies a minimum-neuron criterion for this dataset; the documented curation is the ROI-validity filter, which is already applied via `exclude_invalid_rois=True`. These are genuine recordings of valid ROIs, and the low accuracy in small populations is a real scientific property (few cells carry little decodable information), not an artifact. Removing ~20% of real trials *because they decode poorly* would optimise the reported score rather than the fidelity of the conversion, and would misrepresent the dataset. The evidence is documented here so the trade-off is explicit and the filter can be applied downstream if a user wants it.\n\nTwo further structural reasons the weaker outputs are bounded:\n- **trial_outcome** is constant within a trial, so the decoder must infer it from 8 bins that include 3 pre-change bins carrying no outcome information at all; and the classes are very unbalanced (FA is 1.9% of trials). 14 sessions do not even contain all four outcome classes (12 have 3, 2 have 2) -- a real property of behaviour.\n- **pupil_diameter** is an arousal variable only indirectly reflected in V1/LM activity, and is quantised within session, so the classes are by construction equally likely and cannot be won by a prior.\n\n### Check 2: Accuracy comparison to papers\n| Variable | My validation accuracy | Paper's reported value |\n|---|---|---|\n| image change (change vs repeat) | 0.658 balanced | Figure 6A, **graphical only** -- no numeric value printed in the text; text states changes \"could be decoded equally well for all cell classes\" |\n| hit vs miss | not decoded separately; `trial_outcome` (4-class) = 0.318 | Figure 6C, graphical only; higher for visual than timing sessions |\n| false alarm | part of `trial_outcome`; FA is the rarest class | text: \"false alarm decoding performance was very low\" -- **consistent with my result** |\n\nThe papers report no numeric decoding accuracies (all in figures), so no quantitative discrepancy can be established. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Running speed*?\n\ni. Speed is averaged within each 750 ms bin, using the same cumulative-sum/`searchsorted` machinery as\nthe neural data (sum of samples in `[t0, t1)` divided by the number of samples). If a bin happens to\ncontain no running sample, the value falls back to a linear interpolation of the raw trace at the bin\ncentre, so no NaN can appear. The binned continuous values `(n_trials, 8)` are then discretised (5-c).\nRunning speed is *not* resampled onto the ophys timebase; it is aggregated directly onto the shared\nflash-defined bin windows.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef binned_mean_1d(values, timestamps, t0, t1):\n    \"\"\"Mean of a 1-D signal in each window; empty windows fall back to linear interpolation\n    at the window centre so that no NaN is produced.\"\"\"\n    s, n = binned_sum(values[None, :], timestamps, t0, t1)\n    s = s[0]\n    n = n.astype(float)\n    out = np.empty_like(s)\n    ok = n > 0\n    out[ok] = s[ok] / n[ok]\n    if np.any(~ok):\n        centres = 0.5 * (t0[~ok] + t1[~ok])\n        out[~ok] = np.interp(centres, timestamps, values)\n    return out\n```\n```python\n    run_binned = binned_mean_1d(run_v, run_t, flat_t0, flat_t1).reshape(n_trials, N_BINS)\n```\n\niii. Step 5 variable mapping: \"mean speed within each bin, discretized into 5 equal-percentile bins\".\nThe mean (rather than a point sample) is the natural aggregate when downsampling a 60 Hz signal to\n750 ms bins — ~45 samples per bin. The interpolation fallback exists so that missing samples can never\nproduce NaN, which the format verifier rejects; the AI also asserts finiteness per session\n(`assert np.isfinite(...run_binned).all()`).\n\n## 5-c. How is `output` *Running speed* thresholded into categories?\n\ni. Into 5 equal-percentile classes (quintiles), with the percentile edges computed **within each\nsession** over all bins of all trials of that session, not globally across the dataset. Edges are the\n20/40/60/80th percentiles of the session's binned speeds; assignment is `np.searchsorted(edges, x,\nside='right')`, so ties on an edge go to the upper class and degenerate (repeated) edges simply collapse\none class rather than erroring. The verification log confirms the overall distribution is exactly\n[0.200, 0.200, 0.200, 0.200, 0.200].\n\nii.\n```python\ndef quantile_bin(x, n=N_QUANTILES):\n    \"\"\"Discretise into n equal-percentile bins. Returns integer labels in [0, n-1].\n    Percentile edges are computed on the values being discretised, so each class holds ~1/n\n    of the samples. Ties (e.g. a mouse that is stationary for >20% of the time) can make\n    edges coincide; np.searchsorted then simply assigns fewer samples to the collapsed class.\"\"\"\n    edges = np.quantile(x, np.linspace(0, 1, n + 1)[1:-1])\n    return np.searchsorted(edges, x, side='right').astype(np.int64), edges\n```\n```python\n    run_cls, run_edges = quantile_bin(run_binned.ravel())\n    run_cls = run_cls.reshape(n_trials, N_BINS)\n```\n\niii. Key Decision 7 (quoted in 5-c) makes the pupil-specific argument the primary one: \"pupil width is\nmeasured in camera pixels whose scale depends on the per-session camera alignment ... so a single\nglobal edge set would mostly encode which session/mouse a trial came from rather than the animal\nstate.\" Step 12 adds the consequence for interpretation: \"pupil_diameter is an arousal variable only\nindirectly reflected in V1/LM activity, and is quantised within session, so the classes are by\nconstruction equally likely and cannot be won by a prior.\"\n\n## 6-d.
